excerpt: Differential equations is one of the most predictable scoring chapters in the Class 12 board paper — if you drill the right five problem types in the right order. Here is that order, with worked examples and a quick quiz to test yourself.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Open any CBSE Class 12 maths paper from the last decade and you will find the same thing: differential equations quietly hands out marks to students who practised the standard types, and quietly takes them from students who tried to reason each sum from scratch. This chapter rewards pattern recognition more than raw cleverness. Good worksheets on differential equations for Class 12 are not random question dumps — they march you through the five recognisable forms in the order the syllabus actually builds them, so that by exam day you name the type in seconds and reach for the right method automatically.

Below is exactly that progression, the way I sequence it when I coach board students. Work through it with a pen, not just your eyes. A differential equation you can only follow when someone else solves it is not one you can solve alone at 10 a.m. in the exam hall.

Start with order and degree — the free marks

Before you solve anything, the paper almost always asks you to state the order and degree of a given equation. Order is the highest derivative present; degree is the power of that highest-order derivative once the equation is polynomial in derivatives (free of radicals and fractions on the derivatives). For example, in (d²y/dx²)³ + (dy/dx)² + y = 0 the order is 2 and the degree is 3.

One honest trap the NCERT loves: if the equation has a derivative inside a radical or a trig function — say sin(dy/dx) — the degree is not defined. Students who write ‘degree 1’ out of habit lose an easy mark. Practise ten of these first; they take thirty seconds each and they are guaranteed to appear.

The five methods you must recognise

Almost every solvable Class 12 differential equation falls into one of five buckets. The whole game is identifying which bucket before you write a single step.

TypeHow to spot itMethod
Variable separableYou can split into f(y)dy = g(x)dxIntegrate both sides
Homogeneousdy/dx = F(y/x), all terms same degreeSubstitute y = vx
Linear in ydy/dx + P(x)·y = Q(x)Integrating factor e∫P dx
Linear in xdx/dy + P(y)·x = Q(y)Integrating factor e∫P dy
Forming a DEA family with arbitrary constants is givenDifferentiate, eliminate constants

1. Variable separable

The gentlest type and the one to master first. Take dy/dx = xy. Separate the variables: dy/y = x dx. Integrate: ln|y| = x²/2 + C, so y = A·ex²/2. The only place students slip is forgetting the constant, or dropping the modulus signs. Do not skip either — the board expects the general solution written cleanly.

2. Homogeneous equations

When every term has the same total degree in x and y, write dy/dx = F(y/x) and substitute y = vx, so dy/dx = v + x(dv/dx). This turns a messy equation into a separable one in v and x. For dy/dx = (x + y)/x, the substitution reduces it to x(dv/dx) = 1, which integrates to v = ln|x| + C, giving y = x(ln|x| + C). The substitution y = vx is the single most tested trick in the whole chapter.

3. Linear differential equations (integrating factor)

This is the highest-scoring five- or six-mark type, so give it the most practice. The form is dy/dx + P(x)·y = Q(x). Compute the integrating factor IF = e∫P dx, multiply through, and the left side collapses into d/dx (y · IF). Then y · IF = ∫Q · IF dx + C.

Take dy/dx + (1/x)y = x². Here P = 1/x, so IF = e∫(1/x)dx = eln x = x. Multiplying gives d/dx(xy) = x³, hence xy = x⁴/4 + C. When the equation looks linear in x instead of y, do not force it — swap to dx/dy + P(y)·x = Q(y) and repeat the same machinery.

4. Forming a differential equation

The reverse direction: you are handed a family of curves with n arbitrary constants and asked for the differential equation. The rule is simple — the order of the resulting equation equals the number of arbitrary constants. Differentiate n times and eliminate the constants. From y = mx (one constant), differentiate to get dy/dx = m, then substitute back: x(dy/dx) = y. From y = A·ex + B·e−x (two constants) you will land on a second-order equation, d²y/dx² = y.

How the CBSE actually asks these

The chapter typically carries 8 to 10 marks across a board paper, and the question styles are stable year to year:

  • A 1-mark order/degree identification.
  • A 2-mark variable separable or ‘form the DE’ question.
  • A 3-mark homogeneous equation needing the y = vx substitution.
  • A 5-mark linear DE requiring the integrating factor, often with an initial condition to find C (a particular solution).
  • Increasingly, a case-study block: a real context (cooling of a body, population growth, radioactive decay) that you translate into a DE and solve.

A worksheet progression that works

Do not attempt mixed problems on day one — that only teaches confusion. In my experience the students who jump straight to ‘solve this’ without first drilling identification are the ones who freeze in the exam. A sequence that has served my students well: two days of pure order-degree and separable questions, two days on homogeneous with the y = vx substitution until it is reflex, three days on linear DEs and integrating factors (the heaviest weightage), and a final couple of days on forming DEs plus mixed case-study problems where you must first decide the type. That deciding step is the whole point — it is what the board is really testing.

Test yourself, then practise properly

The quiz below runs through all five types — order and degree, separable, homogeneous, linear, and forming a DE — at exactly board level. Attempt each one on paper before you check, and read every explanation, even for the questions you got right. When you are ready for full-length, exam-style practice, the case-study worksheet e-book at the end gives graded differential equation problems with complete step-by-step solutions and an answer key.

quiz.title: Class 12 Differential Equations Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight board-level questions across order and degree, variable separable, homogeneous, linear DEs and forming a differential equation. Solve each on paper, then press Check my score.

questions.q: Find the order and degree of (d²y/dx²)³ + (dy/dx)² + y = 0.
questions.explanation: The highest derivative is the second, so the order is 2. Its power in the polynomial form is 3, so the degree is 3.

questions.q: What is the integrating factor of dy/dx + (1/x)y = x²?
questions.explanation: Here P = 1/x, so IF = e^(∫(1/x)dx) = e^(ln x) = x.

questions.q: The general solution of dy/dx = sec²x is:
questions.explanation: Integrating sec²x gives tan x, so y = tan x + C.

questions.q: Solving dy/dx = xy by separating variables gives:
questions.explanation: Separate: dy/y = x dx. Integrate: ln|y| = x²/2 + C, so y = A·e^(x²/2).

questions.q: What is the order of the differential equation of the family y = A·eˣ + B·e⁻ˣ?
questions.explanation: There are two arbitrary constants, A and B, so the order of the differential equation equals 2.

questions.q: Which of the following is a linear differential equation?
questions.explanation: A linear DE has the form dy/dx + P(x)·y = Q(x), with y and dy/dx to the first power. Only dy/dx + y = x fits.
Separable: dy/y = −2 dx gives y = C·e⁻²ˣ. Using y(0) = 1 gives C = 1, so y = e⁻²ˣ.

questions.q: Eliminating the arbitrary constant m from y = mx gives which differential equation?
questions.explanation: Differentiate: dy/dx = m. Since m = y/x, substitute to get x·dy/dx = y.

faq.q: How many marks does differential equations carry in the Class 12 board exam?
faq.a: The chapter usually contributes 8 to 10 marks across a CBSE paper, typically split between a short order-degree or separable question, a homogeneous or linear DE for higher marks, and increasingly a case-study block. Its weightage makes it one of the most reliable scoring chapters in the calculus unit.

faq.q: Which type of differential equation should I practise first?
faq.a: Start with order and degree identification, then variable separable equations. They build the habit of writing the constant of integration and handling the general solution cleanly, which every later type depends on. Move to homogeneous and linear DEs only once separable feels automatic.

faq.q: What is the fastest way to spot a linear differential equation?
faq.a: Check whether you can write it as dy/dx + P(x)·y = Q(x), with both y and dy/dx appearing only to the first power and no products like y·(dy/dx). If yes, compute the integrating factor e<sup>∫P dx</sup> and proceed — this single type carries the heaviest marks in the chapter.

faq.q: How do I decide the order when forming a differential equation from a family of curves?
faq.a: The order equals the number of independent arbitrary constants in the family. One constant gives a first-order equation, two constants give a second-order equation, and so on. Differentiate that many times and eliminate the constants to reach the differential equation.
